To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
catchment inputs and sediment focusing can have a significant impact on the reliability of sediment records for atmospherically deposited pollutants.

The mass balance of fallout 210Pb in Brotherswater is complicated by catchment inputs and the transport of fine particulates through the water column that are removed from the lake at relatively slow rates.
the transport and deposition of 210Pbs and 137Cs are complex and that their sediment records may be unreliable for dating.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the role of catchment and water column transport processes on lake records of atmospherically deposited pollutants, with particular reference to fallout radionuclide records used to date sediment cores.
the role of intervening processes in the sedimentation record and the implications this has for the use of lake sediments in reconstructing historical events.
the use of sedimentary archives in the study of environmental change and the development of reliable models of environmental change.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the transport and fate of radionuclids in lakes is a complicated and variable phenomenon, and that simple assumptions regarding the reliability of the sediment record for dating or historical reconstructions of other contaminants may be misleading.
the transport of radionuclids in lakes is complicated, but not so much that simple models are not useful for the purposes of dating.
the transport processes that affect the delivery of 210Pbsediment and 137Csediment records are complex but that they are not sufficiently complex to prevent their use for dating.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

although sediment archives are valuable for reconstructing the history of many environmental processes, their interpretation must take account of the complex transport processes that affect the delivery of these substances from the catchment to the sediment record.

the sediment archive is not a simple one-to-one reflection of the atmosphere, but a complex one that is dependent on the properties and behaviour of the substances in question, and on the physical and chemical properties of the catchment and lake.

the use of sedimentary records of fallout radionumclides as environmental tracers should be undertaken with care and that, where possible, independent information should be used in conjunction with sedimentary records to constrain the interpretation of results.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the reliability of the sediment archive is dependent on the transport characteristics of the substance of interest.
the transport and deposition of these substances in lakes is not as straightforward as might be assumed and that the use of simple models may lead to significant errors.
, in lakes with short water residence times, catchment inputs are likely to be significant and should be accounted for in the interpretation of sediment archives.
